name: Temperance movement
info: The temperance movement was a social movement, strongest in English-speaking, Scandinavian and Protestant countries from the 19th century, that urged moderation in or total abstinence from alcohol and, in many places, laws restricting or prohibiting its sale.

facts.where: the United States, Great Britain and Ireland, the British colonies including Australia, New Zealand and India, Canada, Norway, Finland, Iceland, Russia and France
facts.period: earlier efforts from 1737 and the 1790s; a national movement in the United States from the 1820s; teetotalism from the 1830s; the Washingtonians from 1840; gospel temperance after the American Civil War; a mass movement from the 1860s; national prohibitions in the 1910s and 1920s; decline from the 1930s; still active today
facts.figures: Benjamin Rush, physician who described drinking as a disease; Lyman Beecher, minister who called drunkenness a national sin; John Edgar, Belfast minister; Theobald Mathew, Irish priest; Neal Dow, behind the Maine law of 1851; Frances Willard, second president of the Woman's Christian Temperance Union; Carrie Nation, arrested 30 times; Wayne Wheeler of the Anti-Saloon League
facts.outcome: national prohibitions in Canada, Norway, Finland and the United States, all later repealed, and prohibition in some Indian provinces from 1948 to the present; the movement still exists, with less political influence than in the early 20th century

t: Early societies urged moderate drinking, which is why the movement bears the name temperance; from the 1830s teetotalism demanded complete abstinence, and later reformers sought laws against the sale of alcohol.
By 1900, scholars have estimated, one in ten Americans had signed a pledge to abstain, and the movement became the most well-organised lobby group of its time.

National prohibitions were introduced in Canada, Norway, Finland and the United States between 1918 and 1920 and were repealed, the American one in 1933, after critics pointed to bootlegging, crime and lost tax revenue.
dyk: In 1767 the average New England family was consuming seven barrels of hard cider a year, about 35 gallons per person, in the colonies where the temperance movement later took shape.
ev: The American Temperance Society is formed in Boston, and within 12 years claims more than 8,000 local groups and over 1,250,000 members
Teetotalism originates in Preston, Lancashire, and William Apess founds the first formal Native American temperance society among the Maspee
Artisans in Baltimore found the Washingtonians, who pledge complete abstinence and rely on sympathy for drinkers rather than on law
Maine passes a full-fledged prohibition law, the work of Neal Dow, and several other states follow in the next two decades
A crusade against saloons begins in Ohio, and the Woman's Christian Temperance Union is organised in Cleveland the next year
The Anti-Saloon League begins in Ohio and later campaigns for national prohibition
The Eighteenth Amendment introduces prohibition of the manufacture, sale and distribution of alcoholic beverages in the United States
The Twenty-first Amendment is ratified on 5 December and repeals nationwide prohibition

sections.background:
In late 17th-century North America alcohol was a beverage, a medicine and a commodity for men, women and children. Drinking was widely accepted and integrated into society, although drunkenness was not tolerated. In 1767 the average New England family consumed seven barrels of hard cider a year, about 35 gallons per person. In the early 19th-century United States, water supplies were often polluted, milk was not always available and coffee and tea were expensive, and it was impolite, particularly for men, to refuse alcohol.

Attitudes in Great Britain turned more negative in the late 18th century, in part because the Industrial Revolution needed sober labourers to operate heavy machinery. During the 18th-century gin craze the middle classes grew critical of drunkenness among the lower classes, and in 1743 John Wesley proclaimed that buying, selling and drinking liquor, unless absolutely necessary, were evils to be avoided. Anthony Benezet suggested abstinence in 1775. In the 1790s the physician Benjamin Rush envisioned a disease-like syndrome caused by excessive drinking, with moral and physical decay as its symptoms and abstinence as the only treatment. He condemned distilled spirits but saw benefits in fermented drinks. Abstinence messages were largely ignored by Americans until the 1820s.

Native American activists had begun to campaign against alcohol as early as 1737, after alcohol given in trade for furs had brought poverty and social disintegration to their communities.
sections.aims:
The early societies called for moderate drinking, hence the name temperance, and aimed their advice at hard spirits rather than at all alcohol. In 1826 the minister Lyman Beecher described inebriation as a national sin and suggested laws to prohibit the sale of alcohol. From the 1830s a stricter form, teetotalism, promoted complete abstinence, wine and beer included. The word came from the capital T written beside the names of people who pledged complete abstinence, and teetotallers were known as the pure-water army.

Temperance proponents saw alcohol as the most crucial problem of Western civilisation, a cause of poverty and of all types of social problems. They believed abstinence would reduce crime, strengthen families and improve society as a whole. Temperance advocates used scientific arguments, but at its core the philosophy was moral and religious. One argument held that alcohol enables a few to become rich while it impoverishes the very many. Around the 1900s the ideal of strong citizens developed into a hygienism, which held that heredity carried drinking problems to later generations.

Ideas on how to restrict consumption were varied and conflicting: prohibition by law, a state monopoly on all alcohol sales, or reform of the law to remove profit from the alcohol industry. Temperance organisations also promoted alcohol education and ran sobriety lectures, reform clubs, temperance hotels and petition campaigns.
sections.events:
In 1810 Calvinist ministers met in a seminary in Massachusetts to write articles on abstinence for their sermons, and the Massachusetts Society for the Suppression of Intemperance was formed in 1813; it accepted only men of high social standing, peaked in 1818 and ended in 1820. The American Temperance Society was formed in Boston in 1826 and within 12 years claimed more than 8,000 local groups and over 1,250,000 members. In 1829 the Presbyterian minister John Edgar of Belfast poured his stock of whiskey out of his window. Teetotalism originated in Preston, Lancashire, in 1833, and the Irish priest Theobald Mathew established the Teetotal Abstinence Society in 1838.

In 1840 artisans in Baltimore formed the Washingtonians, who pledged complete abstinence and won others through their own experience rather than preaching. By 1845 they had lost prominence: evangelical reformers attacked them for refusing to call alcoholism a sin, many men returned to drinking, and the movement divided over prohibition laws. The Band of Hope, founded in Leeds in 1847 to teach working-class children sobriety, became a national organisation in 1855. The Maine law of 1851 was followed by bans in several other states, and organised opposition led five of twelve states with prohibition laws to eliminate or weaken them.

During the winter of 1873 to 1874 a crusade of over 32,000 women stormed saloons and liquor stores in the Midwest, and the Woman's Christian Temperance Union was organised in Cleveland in November 1874. The Anti-Saloon League began in Ohio in 1893 and began its efforts for national prohibition in 1913.
sections.people:
Benjamin Rush saw drunkenness as a disease and called on ministers to preach temperance. Charles Grandison Finney taught abstinence from ardent spirits, and at the Rochester, New York, revival of 1831 individuals were required to sign a temperance pledge to receive salvation. The Pequot writer and minister William Apess founded a Native American temperance society among the Maspee on 11 October 1833. Neal Dow was behind the Maine law of 1851. Abraham Lincoln addressed the Springfield Washington Temperance Society on 22 February 1842, criticising early methods as overly forceful and praising the Washingtonians. Jabez Tunnicliff founded the Band of Hope.

Women were central. By 1831 there were over 24 women's temperance organisations. Amelia Bloomer, Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony were active in temperance and abolitionist movements in the 1840s, and Anthony stated that women suffer the most from drunkenness. Frances Willard, the second president of the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, helped make it the largest women's religious organisation of the 19th century and was also interested in suffrage and women's rights. Carrie Nation, one of the most extreme workers, was arrested 30 times for what she called hatchetations, destroying property in bars, saloons and even pharmacies.

Wayne Wheeler of the Anti-Saloon League covered legislators' desks with telegrams, a method called Wheelerism, and the Cincinnati Enquirer called him the strongest political force of his day.
sections.outcomes:
By the 1910s half the countries in the world had introduced some form of alcohol control. Iceland introduced prohibition in 1915 and liberalised spirits in 1933, though beer stayed illegal until 1989. Canada had national prohibition from 1918 to 1920, Norway banned spirits from 1919 to 1926 and Finland had prohibition from 1919 to 1932, repealed after an upsurge in violent crime associated with the illegal liquor trade. The United States ratified the Eighteenth Amendment in 1920 and repealed it in 1933 with the Twenty-first. Some provinces in India have had prohibition from 1948 to the present.

Prohibition had some positive effects at first. Henry Ford reported that absenteeism in his companies had halved, and alcohol consumption fell dramatically. Against this, thousands of jobs were lost, the catering and entertainment industries lost profits, tax revenues fell, with some estimates at 11 billion dollars for the United States, and enforcement was expensive. The Eighteenth Amendment did not prohibit consumption, so illegal consumption became commonplace. Illegally produced alcohol killed a thousand people a year, and bootlegging was profitable. Crime rose rather than fell, contrary to what proponents had expected.

Opposition came from German and Irish immigrants, who considered drinking part of their cultures. In 1872 the Chicago bosses A. C. Hesing and Hermann Raster forced the Republican Party to adopt an anti-temperance platform. In the United States the movement declined as fundamentalist and nativist groups became dominant in it, which led moderate members to leave.
sections.legacy:
The temperance movement still exists in many parts of the world but is generally less politically influential than in the early 20th century. Active organisations include the World Woman's Christian Temperance Union, Mothers Against Drunk Driving, Alcohol Justice, International Blue Cross, the Independent Order of Rechabites and the International Organisation of Good Templars. Groups such as the Woman's Christian Temperance Union support warning labels on alcoholic drinks. The Salvation Army and the Allegheny Wesleyan Methodist Connection still require members to refrain from alcohol.

The movement produced its own popular culture: periodicals, temperance theatre from the 1820s, and songs by writers such as George Frederick Root, Henry Clay Work and Stephen C. Foster. Temperance halls, bars and coffee palaces replaced saloons, and Mr Fitzpatrick's in Lancashire is thought to be the oldest temperance bar. In 1901 American schools were required to teach temperance, though the instruction was accused of spreading misinformation, fear mongering and racist stereotypes. The Word of Wisdom, a health code of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints that some scholars think was influenced by the movement, was the basis of a call in 1921 from Heber J. Grant for the Latter-day Saints to adhere strictly to it, including complete abstinence from alcohol.

In colonial India the movement tied in with the independence movement, since Mahatma Gandhi viewed alcohol as a foreign importation. In the 1990s temperance was part of the straight edge scene. In Tamil Nadu in 2016 many women voted for a pro-prohibition leader, Jayaram Jayalalithaa, who shut five hundred liquor shops on her first day in office.

summary: The temperance movement urged moderation in, then abstinence from, alcohol, and later laws against its sale, from the 1820s in the United States and Britain and then across many countries. It won national prohibitions in the 1910s and 1920s, mostly repealed, and it still exists.
references: Brian Harrison, Drink & the Victorians, the Temperance question in England 1815–1872 (Faber and Faber, 1971)
Ian Tyrrell, Woman's World/Woman's Empire: The Woman's Christian Temperance Union in International Perspective, 1880–1930 (University of North Carolina Press, 1991)
notes: Start 1820 (circa) is a choice: the article says the American movement began at a national level in the 1820s, but also dates Native American activism to 1737 and Rush to the 1790s. Event list begins 1826 (American Temperance Society).

The article says the Anti-Saloon League's leader was Susan B. Anthony and that it campaigned for suffrage; this is at odds with the rest of the article (Wayne Wheeler, 1913 national campaign) and I left it out. Anthony is mentioned only for her remark on women and drunkenness.
The article gives 1.5 million members for the American Temperance Union by 1835 and 1,250,000 for the American Temperance Society within 12 years; I used only the latter.
The article states that alcohol consumption in the US halved between 1830 and 1840 and also that drinking increased until after 1830; left out.
Prohibition in 'twelve US states', five of which weakened it, is given in the article without a year; I wrote it as given. 'Prohibition laws' in Massachusetts 1838 left out.
Odd text in the article ('Was this in England or Ireland?' after Edgar) is an editorial insertion; I said only Belfast, as the article's description of Edgar does.

Left out: the Latter-day Saints' Joseph Smith discussion, Millerites, Adventists, Chartism's temperance current, Russia's war prohibition, France's L'Alarme, the Scottish Prohibition Party, Bihar, statistics quoted for Bihar, and the Pompili health figures, for length or because they are claims the editor may wish to add.
